newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish people see no change from Major statement.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish people see no change from Major statement.

text.p: Catholics and Protestants in Northern Ireland were in rare agreement on one thing on Friday: British Prime Minister John Major's latest posture on an IRA ceasefire had done nothing to help matters.
"Nothing has changed. It's the same rubbish all the time," said one Christmas shopper in Belfast's city centre.

Major on Thursday spelled out the steps he thought necessary for the IRA's political branch, Sinn Fein, to join talks on the future of Northern Ireland. But he also repeated his insistence that the Irish Republican Army must first declare an "unequivocal" truce in its guerrilla war against Britain.
The Independent newspaper called Major's remarks an "olive twig." But republicans, who want a truce to guarantee them immediate entry into the forum, rejected the overture.
Catholics in Belfast said they believed Major must go further if he is to avert more violence by the IRA, which abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in its fight for a united Ireland last February.
"He needs to grant them some concessions, perhaps release some IRA prisoners, to keep them talking," said a middle-aged man, huddling out of the wind in a doorway.

"I personally want a united Ireland, but this is not the way to go about it, this silly war. Major needs to keep them talking for perhaps two or three years and then it would be too hard for them to go back to war."
Another, younger, Catholic said: "I think he's just trying to push them for more bombs."
But an elderly Protestant couple believed Major was being tough with Sinn Fein, and was right to be so.
"He's quite right. He should never talk to them anyway," said the husband. "Ignore them," chimed in his wife.
Belfast's city centre was crowded in the run-up to Christmas.

Largely thanks to a huge influx of funds from mainland Britain, the city's pristine pavements and bright shop windows belie the its violent past and the bombs that repeatedly reduced buildings to rubble.
Since ending its truce, the IRA has carried out only one attack in the province, on the British army's headquarters at Lisburn, south of Belfast. One person was killed.
Now political analysts are unsure whether moderate elements in the republican movement will be able to dissuade hardliners from resuming their battle.
"Its not clear whether the softliners will be able to hold them (IRA hardliners) back," said Brendan O'Leary, professor of political science at the London School of Economics.

O'Leary was sceptical of the view that Major had offered concessions to the IRA, believing instead that the prime minister had bowed to pressure from the pro-British Unionists on whom he relies for support in parliament.
"Major has decided to stay in parliament for the next five months rather than seek an agreement," said O'Leary.
The Irish News agreed, carrying a cartoon of Major in parliament with the caption; "I must remind certain gentlemen that I'm strictly in this for the short haul."
